𝐂𝐚𝐧 𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐨𝐭𝐬 𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝 𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬?

Last fall Monumental was asked to build a small transformer box near The Hague. The drawings called for vertical "soldier course" bricks — something we'd 𝘯𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳 done. Oh, also just 2 weeks until deployment.

Three problems, three pragmatic answers:

🧱 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 — our grid-based wall design assumed horizontal bricks. Vertical bricks broke the alignment math. Reworked the grid so soldier-course joints align cleanly with the horizontal ones.

🤖 𝐕𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 — our pick-quality neural net only knew horizontal bricks. Plan A was retraining. Plan B exploited the known orientation, slid an expected bounding box along the stereo depth map, and picked the best fit. Plan B was deployable in days, so we shipped it.

🛠️ 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐝𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 — neither the supply robot nor the gripper could rotate a brick. A new actuator was the "right" answer and weeks of work. Instead: a passive ramp on the supply robot that uses gravity to tip the brick vertical as it leaves the carrier. 3D-printed → tuned → metal → deployed.

Full write-up from our forward-deployed engineer Alexander Agudelo, who led the work: https://lnkd.in/eQRPugS8

content:
I’m excited to share our oversubscribed $32 million round led by Khosla Ventures

This is a moment to reflect on how we reached this point from an engineering and deployment perspective. There is tremendous excitement around robotics, but we often overlook what it takes to turn an idea into a deployed, reliable, revenue-generating product. It involves far more than connecting a few actuators and implementing the latest research in AI vision models and SLAM.

Getting here meant solving the challenges required to deliver the brickwork for 100(!) homes, a school, a community and sports center, a hotel, commercial units, hundreds of meters of Amsterdam’s canal walls, and more:

We built Atrium, our operating system for construction, using Rust, TypeScript, and WebGL. Atrium transforms architectural drawings into robot-executable plans in 3D. It coordinates where humans and robots need to be at any moment, making construction software-defined for the first time.

Construction presents a unique localization challenge: everything must be placed in a precise, one-of-a-kind location, often with almost no nearby reference points. Add to that the fact that the real world rarely matches the blueprint. So where do you put the very first brick? It’s much harder than placing objects in a dishwasher or brightly lit boxes on a conveyor belt.

We’ve spent hours mastering calibration, the real test of whether a robotic fleet can scale. Keeping camera lenses, IMUs, and robot kinematics precisely calibrated is challenging enough in a controlled environment. Doing it reliably across a fleet under constantly changing field conditions is another challenge altogether.

Being obsessed with delivery means taking responsibility for the entire process of building a wall, not just picking and placing bricks. That started with extruding mortar (hard!), but has grown into a suite of tools that allows our robot to autonomously point walls and insert wall ties (really hard!). Both are essential to building structurally sound walls. Visit our website and watch the videos. It’s incredible to see!

As in every fast-growing startup, everything is moving quickly from 1 to N. We’ve gone from a single robot to an entire fleet, from one construction site to multiple concurrent sites, and from operating in one country to a multi-country operation.

Our engineering team has scaled alongside it, growing from 20 to 35 people in the past year. And we continue to hire across the board: software engineers working in robotics, controls, computer vision, backend, and frontend; Forward Deployed Robotics Engineers; Hardware Engineers; and many more roles across operations, delivery, and GTM.

I’m grateful to our team, customers, and investors who helped us reach this point. Thank you to Vinod Khosla and Nico at Khosla Ventures for believing in us and leading this round; to Sten and the amazing team at Plural; and to Firat and Barend at Hummingbird Ventures for supporting us from the earliest days.w

content:
Today we’re announcing Monumental’s oversubscribed $32M Series B, led by Khosla Ventures, with Plural and Hummingbird Ventures.

When I joined a year ago, we were 50 people. Our robots could build a nice wall. The open question was whether they could do it at scale: on messy construction sites, building actual homes. Twelve months later, we’ve delivered the brickwork for:

• More than 100 homes
• A school, a community center, a sports center, a hotel, commercial units
• Hundreds of meters of Amsterdam’s canal walls

Half of that went up in the last three months.

Most autonomy companies spend years in the lab, making impressive videos. We make those too (you’re watching one). Ours are just filmed on real construction sites, for real customers, and we only get paid when the wall is finished.

What’s next: scaling the fleet and deployments while increasing every robot’s output and autonomy. Continuing our expansion in the UK, while launching in the US later this year. Moving into new construction trades, in parallel.

I joined after hearing Salar say at an event that Monumental will become the world’s largest construction company. One that builds things that last, while there aren’t enough hands, productivity has been flat for decades, and our cities have grown uglier because of both. 

The ugliness is the part we’re already reversing. Curved walls, custom color patterns, masonry specials: craft that was vanishing because the hands for it are gone. For our robots, it’s a software tweak.

The team has tripled in the past year (including Daan, a close friend I talked into joining, which I recommend). We’re still hiring: hardware engineers, software engineers, ops, deployments, workshop, robot operators and GTM in the Netherlands, the UK, and the US.

Something surprising happens almost every time we show a general contractor what we do.

They expect the robots to be the showstopper. Autonomous machines laying brick on a live site, that's the part everyone assumes will blow them away. And they are impressed by them. But it's almost never the thing they can't stop talking about.

The moment we open up Atrium and show them the sheer amount of data and planning underneath a build, you can see it click. This is the thing the industry has been missing for so long. Construction runs on billions of dollars and impossibly tight timelines, and yet so much of it is still coordinated on printed out drawings with post-it notes and red marker. Seeing it actually instrumented is a genuinely different experience.

Atrium gives you the whole build at once: the big picture of how it's progressing, whether you're on track, whether you're going to deliver on time. That view alone is more than most sites have ever had.

But then you can keep going, all the way down to a single brick.

You can click on any brick in the wall and see how it got there. The computer vision recognizing and picking it up. Video of it being laid. Every brick in the wall has a record. And at the end, we can hand the contractor a report on the actual quality of what we built, brick by brick. Nobody in construction has ever been able to do that.

The best part is that Atrium is never finished. Our team is innovating on it constantly, and over the years it's grown into the operating system for construction.

I love this video the team put together (John Turpin, Tobias Cornille, Alfred Polycarpe, Paula Wulkop, Lucas Le Faucheur and Martha Fantom). We spent a good part of the conversation on why I think construction is one of the biggest and most underrated problems in the world, because it sits upstream of two things almost everyone feels, namely a severe shortage of skilled labour and a housing crisis that follows directly from it. There simply aren't enough bricklayers to build what the world needs, and with an aging workforce that retires far earlier than most other trades and not nearly enough young people coming in behind them, that gap is only getting wider.
 
What excites me is that this is exactly the gap our robots are already working on, deployed as subcontractors on real sites today rather than waiting for some future where the technology is finished. The need is urgent right now, and the shortage isn't going to wait for us to feel ready.
 
The part I care about just as deeply is that solving this doesn't have to mean cheap and identical buildings. A lot of people trying to fix construction reach straight for prefab sameness. It would be a real loss if that became our entire built environment. We're so much richer than we were a century ago and yet in many ways we're building worse, and what genuinely excites me is that robotics gives us a way to bring craft and beauty back rather than trading them away for scale.

content:
Every single Olympics goes massively over budget (to the tune of, on average, triple the cost).

Yet people hosting the Olympics consistently believe that somehow, this time, it will be different. And they will fight you when you point out the obvious!

One reason for this failure to pattern-detect stems because the Olympics only happens once every four years. It’s rare for people to learn in circumstances of infrequent iteration, which is a good characterization of the cadence of the Olympics.

There’s also a broader psychological bias at play in these types of defensive responses: a lack of cognitive maturity. People would rather make up excuses or pretend a phenomenon doesn’t exist than confront it frankly.

A more granular example was the Crossrail project in the UK that had a whole chunk of system integration missing from their schedule.

The first management team believed, in spite of the evidence in front of them, that the system integration piece was just going to magically get done.

When the project controls team pointed out that the system integration piece was not going to go away, and thus the project was beginning to run late, what did the management team do? They layered political bias on top of psychological bias and fired the project controls team altogether.

If you’re shooting the messenger, there’s a good chance you’re in the magical world of a cognitively immature organization.

If, instead, you’re listening to uncomfortable truths and responding to them in a proactive manner, you’re in the realistic world of a cognitively mature organization - where, by the way, you’ll be more action- and solution-oriented.

Project leaders have two choices. They can let their projects succumb to the compounding failures of internal psychological and political biases, or they can build a culture that invites and rewards the uncomfortable truth-tellers.

Successful projects go out of their way to seek the bad news earlier.

In the data center race right now, there is no silver medal.

Vacancy rates for data centers are under 1 percent, down from 2 percent a year ago. Whatever gets built gets leased almost immediately. Capital isn't the constraint either; over a trillion dollars are currently flowing into this asset class. The only thing separating winners from everyone else is who opens first.

Here's what that actually costs in numbers: 

A 100-megawatt data center runs about a billion dollars to build, financed against a 15-year lease. One month of delay costs roughly 20 million dollars in lost revenue, labor, and penalties. Stretch that delay to six months and the damage lands at roughly 10 percent of the entire project's cost, enough to turn a 15-year lease into 15 years of running the asset just to break even, not to actually profit from it.

I had a professor at Harvard, Clayton M. Christensen, who used to say that if a resource is abundant, it's fine to waste some of it. Right now, capital is abundant. Time is not. The exchange rate most companies are missing is simple: how much is a month of delay actually costing you?

Once you can answer that in hard numbers, delay stops being an operational inconvenience and becomes what it actually is: the single biggest lever on your return.

content:
The most disciplined time management operation I have ever watched did not happen at a construction site. It belongs to Formula 1.

Our team spent Grand Prix week in Monaco this year, close enough to see how a race is actually run.

Racing has been a data sport for decades. But what began with a stopwatch and a clipboard is now hundreds of sensors on a single car, streaming millions of readings to a dedicated crew. 

Everything from tyre degradation to fuel burn, brake temperature, and even the driver's heart rate is measured and accounted for. A strategist can call a pit stop a lap early because the numbers, not the driver, said so.

Most drivers are data-obsessed as well. Former World Champion Nico Rosberg has described managing his bodyweight to the gram before a race in order to keep a more predictable power-to-weight ratio of the car underneath him.

The precision is extraordinary, and entirely unemotional. A race is won or lost by data, decisions, and time.

And that instinct is almost entirely absent from major building projects.

The same companies building billion-dollar data centers have nothing resembling an F1 team's time operation. No one owns the schedule with that kind of rigor, and there’s no agreed standard for what good looks like. 

Optimism about completion dates rests on no evidence at all.

Construction and racing look like opposites. High-vis versus fireproof suits, job sites versus pit lanes. But the cost of a lost minute is just as real on one as the other.

Formula 1 built a discipline around that fact a long time ago. Construction, for the most part, still hasn't.

I spent the start of my career at the World Bank on a belief I've since abandoned: that poverty is a capital problem.

It's an appealing idea because it's actionable. Move enough money into a country, infrastructure follows, prosperity follows that. I worked on the financing side of that equation for years before I noticed how often the money arrived and the infrastructure didn't.

I was wrong about the mechanism, not the goal. Capital is globally abundant. What's scarce is the capability to execute it: the project management discipline that turns financing into a power plant, or a road that holds up, delivered close to the date someone promised. A country can have every dollar it needs and still sit in the dark for want of that discipline.

That distinction has shaped everything I've done since. If execution is the real constraint, then the highest-leverage work isn't building the pipeline to fund. It's building the capability to deliver.

Where does your organization actually sit: short on capital, or short on the discipline to deploy it well?

The obvious objection is that this is an emerging-markets story. It's not. Wealthy countries overrun at the same rate. The gap between what leaders set out to build and what actually gets built turns up everywhere, however deep the pockets.

content:
There’s evidence of Roman emperors writing anxious letters to their generals about aqueducts running over budget.

Two thousand years on, we just use different words for the same trouble. Overrun, delay, and misplaced confidence are as old as ambitious building itself.

I have spent my career studying megaprojects because they are what I would call stable phenomena - systems where past observations can reasonably predict future events.

In modern data centers and Roman settlements alike, you’ll find overconfidence, optimism bias, and political pressure. All human constants, and no political system has ever legislated them away.

The all-too-human aspects of building do not surprise me anymore. But, sitting where I do between research and technology, the speed of change around these human variables is almost shocking.

Five years ago, when I started studying data centers seriously, a rack drew around two kilowatts. Today it is closer to 55. A 100-kilowatt rack was a lab fantasy a year ago and sits in production now.

But even at a breakneck pace, technology can't outrun human bias. Our judgment depends on experience, and the faster technology moves, the less experience we have to draw on. Bias fills that gap instead.

Robert McNamara called this the fog of war, the point where uncertainty grows so thick you can no longer see through it. The harder it becomes to forecast, the more we tend to lean on optimism (justified or not).

That is why stable phenomena invite study. They do not change. Understand the bias and you can design for it, building the governance and the guardrails in advance.

Assume the technology has made you immune, and the aqueduct will tell you otherwise.

content:
One of my uncles was a very famous Urdu poet called Ahmad Faraz.

He used to pick my cousin and me up from school, and we’d have long conversations in the car. He always smoked, and intermittently he’d dip his cigarette in a little glass of water (I always found that very curious) as he spoke to us. It was a little bit of a poetic salon on wheels.

I think of him often now, as I also think of all the other interesting people in my family - the politicians, builders, and entrepreneurs. 

These different types who composed my childhood world helped me come to the realization, later in life, that all organizations need both poetry and plumbing to succeed.

The poet supplies the poetry, the builder supplies the plumbing, the politician supplies the ability to communicate and build relationships. All these things have to go hand in hand.

The penny dropped for me when I started teaching a case study in Singapore Airlines as part of my MBA course at Oxford.

I wanted to discuss the notion of ambidexterity in organizations (i.e. exhibiting the best of both plumbing and poetry), and Singapore Airlines proved to be the perfect example. 

First, it has a lower cost of provision per kilometer than EasyJet’s, which is incredibly surprising for a luxury airline. How did they pull that off? With great plumbing: careful thinking about their fleet, their maintenance, training of young graduates, overhead, software, etc. They’re methodical about their cost structure so that they can spend good money on high quality food and beverage and newer aircraft.

Second, the poetry. When Lee Kuan Yew first became prime minister of Singapore, after it had been expelled from Malaysia, he gave a teary interview vowing that he would convert Singapore from a little fishing village into a global metropolis. Building an airline was part of that poetic mission, as it provided connectivity between this little place and the rest of the world.

Whenever I see an organization successfully combining poetry and plumbing, I think of my uncle, and of all the poetic salons he held in the car. A poetic vision, he implied with his worldview, was the starting point.

Bring it in harmony with great plumbing, and you have something propulsive.

Skiing got me hooked on a detail I now can't unsee in project work.

The best skiers I've watched aren't separated from average ones by one dramatic move. They're separated by an obsessive attention to micro-adjustments — edge angle, weight transfer, the tiny corrections most people don't even register as happening.

Megaprojects reward the same instinct, and punish its absence in the same way. Executives are drawn to the macro picture almost by design — it's what gets reported upward, what gets a slide in the board deck. But the projects that actually stay on track are run by people who also have a handle on the micro: the small variances nobody thought worth escalating, until they'd already compounded.

Elite performance, in sport or in delivery, isn't one big skill. It's the discipline of staying on top of the small ones.

Standardization and innovation get treated as opposites. They aren't.

I made this case on The Peggy Smedley Show a few months ago with two examples.

First: a friend of mine works at a three-Michelin-star restaurant in London. The paradox of that world is that every plate has to come out identical, service after service. Nothing left to chance. Getting to that exact, repeatable dish takes relentless upfront innovation.

Second, further back: IBM in the early 1960s. An earlier defense computing project with MIT had failed. Rather than patch around the wreckage, the team rebuilt the architecture from scratch. What came out the other side was the System/360, a direct ancestor of the modern computer, including the device most people are reading this post on right now.

Data centers and large infrastructure are at a similar point. The industry still treats every project as a one-off, bespoke build. Until it embraces modular, repeatable design the way computing did sixty years ago, it will keep re-solving the same problems from zero, every time.

Standardization isn't the enemy of innovation. It's usually the output of it.

content:
Every serious company has a CFO, but I don't know a single organization with a Chief Time Officer.

Think about the iron triangle of any major project: physical scope, cost, and time. Companies assign clear ownership to cost. If you're building a 100-megawatt data center on a billion-dollar budget with an 18-month timeline, you will have a guaranteed maximum price contract. You will have a CFO who owns every dollar of that billion.

But you will almost certainly not have anyone whose job is to own that 18 months with equivalent rigor.

Organizations didn't develop sophisticated financial management overnight. It took roughly a century of standards, accounting practices, and discipline built around one dimension of business performance. 

Time, by contrast, has had almost none of that institutional development. As a result, it is rarely managed with the same discipline.

If I were to build the Chief Time Officer role from the ground up, it would rest on three pillars:

First: create high-quality schedules that align with industry standards. Not window dressing, or what a colleague of mine aptly calls "sham reporting” or schedules that exist to pretend things are on track. You need schedules that reflect the actual construction sequence and surface exactly what is and isn't working.

Second: control against those schedules with evidence. The CFO equivalent is invoices and bank records. The Chief Time Officer equivalent is documentary evidence at every stage. Is that drawing complete? Has that purchase order been issued? Has that permit been submitted? Evidence, not optimism.

Third: turn schedule data into decisions. CFOs use financial data to drive forecasts and strategy. A Chief Time Officer would use time data the same way: identifying where you need to accelerate, where recovery is needed, and where the plan has to change.

The role of Chief Time Officer doesn't exist yet. But in data centers, in construction, in any environment where three months' delay wipes out net present value, the need is there.

If we want to build more efficient, more profitable megaprojects, we will start by giving time the same seat at the table that money has.

Roughly four in five megaprojects fail.

By that I mean they don’t produce value in terms of cost, time, or the benefit they were built to deliver.

Andy Grove had a phrase for this kind of simplistic appraisal: "Yes, no, simple." He arrived in the United States from Hungary knowing almost no English, so he learned to strip every question to the bone. The habit stayed with him through Intel and everything he wrote about management.

Apply his standard to megaprojects and the metric for failure is simple: did you deliver what you said, for the price you said, when you said it?

80% don’t. But what helps the other 20% of projects avoid this fate? 

After two decades studying them, I can tell you their success has almost nothing to do with budget or technology. It comes down to cognitive maturity, and it shows up as two habits:

The first is true open-mindedness. These teams invite outside eyes in. They do not hide behind confidentiality, which is usually a polite word for being too embarrassed to say what is really happening. Come to the site, they say. Look at the data. See for yourself.

The second is hard realism. They budget for overruns. They picture the bad outcomes in advance and make provisions for them. They plan for failure as carefully as they plan for success.

The unsuccessful teams only visualize the good outcomes, guard their information, and resist any input that might challenge them. They are, in a word, magical in their thinking.

Plan only for success and something breaks. Plan for failure, then execute anyway. That is what the successful 20% understand.

What does Amazon know on the 2nd of the month that most competitors won't until the 21st?

Well, effectively everything. Hundreds of millions of microtransactions, reconciled against revenue, purchase orders, and bank statements by internal AI workflows, in roughly the time it takes to run a management meeting, without the armies of bookkeepers.

The instinct is to file this under cost reduction, which is the small version of the story. 

Amazon didn't automate reconciliation to save money on accountants (that's a different post); instead, it turned the finance function into a live instrument that can move pricing, inventory, and capital against numbers that are hours, not weeks, old. Sounds pretty great to me!

Of course, I see the same pattern in infrastructure, where project controls report monthly, and teams spend most of every month managing something they cannot currently see.
